questions.question: Describe the internal structure of the earth from the surface to the centre, giving for each layer its approximate depth, composition and physical state.
questions.expected_answer: The crust is the thin outer shell of silicate rock, between about 5 and 70 kilometres thick and solid; its base is the Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho. Below it the mantle extends to about 2 900 kilometres, made of dense iron- and magnesium-rich silicate rock, chiefly peridotite. It is solid, but in its upper part — roughly 100 to 250 kilometres down — the asthenosphere is close enough to melting to behave plastically and flow very slowly. At the Gutenberg discontinuity the core begins, composed of iron and nickel. The outer core, from about 2 900 to 5 150 kilometres, is liquid, and its circulating molten metal generates the earth's magnetic field. From 5 150 kilometres to the centre at 6 371 kilometres lies the solid inner core, the hottest place in the earth at some 5 000 to 6 000 degrees Celsius, kept solid by the immense pressure. Temperature, pressure and density all increase with depth.

questions.question: Compare continental and oceanic crust, and explain why oceanic crust subducts when the two converge.
questions.expected_answer: Continental crust, traditionally called sial after its dominant silica and aluminium, is 30 to 50 kilometres thick and up to 70 beneath major mountain ranges. It is granitic in composition, relatively light at about 2,7 grams per cubic centimetre, and very old — some of it close to four billion years, as in South Africa's Kaapvaal Craton. Oceanic crust, or sima, is only 5 to 10 kilometres thick, basaltic in composition, denser at about 3,0 grams per cubic centimetre, and nowhere older than roughly 200 million years, because it is continuously created at mid-ocean ridges and destroyed at subduction zones. When the two converge, the denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the lighter continental one. Subduction is therefore a consequence of buoyancy rather than an arbitrary rule, and it explains why deep ocean trenches lie against continental margins.

questions.question: We have never drilled deeper than about 12 kilometres. Explain how seismic waves nevertheless allow us to establish the state of the earth's interior.
questions.expected_answer: Every large earthquake sends body waves through the whole planet, and the two types behave differently. P-waves are compressional, fastest, and travel through solids, liquids and gases alike. S-waves are transverse and cannot pass through liquid at all, because a liquid has no rigidity to transmit a sideways shear. Seismic stations worldwide record every large earthquake, and beyond about 103 degrees from the epicentre no S-waves arrive anywhere — an S-wave shadow zone. Their complete absence, rather than mere weakening, proves that they met a liquid layer, so the outer core must be molten. P-waves are not stopped but are sharply refracted where they cross from the solid mantle into the liquid outer core, producing a further shadow zone between roughly 103 and 143 degrees whose size gives the depth of the core-mantle boundary. Faint arrivals within that zone, refracted again at the Lehmann discontinuity, reveal a solid inner core. Three supporting arguments confirm the picture: the whole earth's average density of about 5,5 grams per cubic centimetre far exceeds the 2,7 of surface rock, so the interior must be metallic; a planetary magnetic field requires circulating liquid metal; and iron meteorites match the composition the core must have.
